guide.title: Head & Brain Injury
guide.lead: You can't fix the injury from the impact, but you can stop the second one. Prevent hypoxia, hypotension and over-ventilation, then get the patient to neurosurgery. One episode of low oxygen or low BP can double the damage.

sections.title: Protect the brain
rows: Systolic at least 110 mmHg in most adults
Head of stretcher up 30° if the spine allows
Tight collars, lying flat with vomiting

sections.title: Signs of herniation?
sections.question: Falling GCS with a blown pupil, extensor posturing or Cushing's triad?
items: Cushing's triad: rising BP, slowing pulse, irregular breathing
sections.yes: Brief hyperventilation to EtCO₂ 30–35 mmHg (adult about 20 breaths/min, child 25, infant 30) as a bridge; pre-alert neurosurgery.

groups.title: Epidural
items: Arterial; lucid interval, then rapid decline

groups.title: Subdural
items: Venous; slower; older adults, alcohol, anticoagulants

groups.title: Basal skull fracture
items: Raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, CSF from nose or ears

groups.title: Sport concussion
items: Remove from play; no return the same day
Helmet stays on unless the airway needs it

quiz.q: GCS E1 V1 M2 = 4 after a motorcycle crash. Interpretation?
options: Severe TBI with extensor posturing: trauma centre with neurosurgery; prevent secondary injury

quiz.q: Brief unconsciousness, then talking, then drowsy, vomiting and a fixed dilated right pupil. Most likely?
On warfarin, hit her head, GCS 14 and "a little confused". Management?
options: Transport for CT: high risk of intracranial bleeding
quiz.explanation: Any anticoagulated head injury needs a scan.

quiz.q: GCS 6, no signs of herniation. Ventilation rate (adult)?
Minimum systolic BP target in adult TBI:

options: Rising BP, slowing pulse, irregular breathing
Low BP, fast pulse, fast breathing
quiz.explanation: A late sign of rising pressure.

quiz.q: Severe TBI is a GCS of:
quiz.explanation: They often can't protect their airway.

quiz.q: Herniation signs: brief hyperventilation target EtCO₂:
A footballer is confused after a hit but wants to play on:
options: Remove from play; no return the same day
Let him play if he feels better

quiz.q: Head-injured adult with BP 84/56 and pale, cool skin:
options: Look for bleeding elsewhere: head injury rarely causes shock
Lower the head of the stretcher

flashcards.question: Skull fractures
flashcards.answer: Linear, depressed, basal. Basal signs: raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, CSF from nose or ears, blood behind the eardrum.

flashcards.question: Primary vs secondary brain injury
flashcards.answer: Primary: at impact, irreversible. Secondary: from hypoxia, hypotension, glucose problems and raised pressure – preventable.

flashcards.question: Cushing's triad
flashcards.answer: Rising BP (widening pulse pressure), bradycardia, irregular breathing: late sign of raised intracranial pressure.

flashcards.question: GCS ranges
flashcards.answer: Eyes 1–4, verbal 1–5, motor 1–6 (total 3–15). Mild 13–15, moderate 9–12, severe 8 or less.

flashcards.question: Lucid interval
flashcards.answer: Normal consciousness after injury, then rapid decline: classic for epidural hematoma.

flashcards.question: Epidural vs subdural
flashcards.answer: Epidural: arterial, rapid. Subdural: venous, slower; older adults, alcohol use, anticoagulants.

flashcards.question: Signs of herniation
flashcards.answer: Falling GCS, unequal or fixed dilated pupil, extensor posturing, Cushing's triad.

flashcards.question: Ventilation in TBI
flashcards.answer: Normally EtCO₂ 35–45 mmHg (adult about 10 breaths/min). With herniation signs only: briefly to 30–35 mmHg (adult about 20 breaths/min).

critical.scenario: Fell 20 feet; GCS 12 then dropping. BP rises to 168/82, pulse 56, irregular breathing 8/min. Right pupil 6 mm and fixed; right-sided extension to pain.
critical.question: What's happening and what now?

options.t: Herniation: secure the airway, ventilate to EtCO₂ 30–35 mmHg as a bridge, head up 30°, emergency transport to neurosurgery
A seizure: glucose and recovery position
options.f: Cushing's triad and a blown pupil mean herniation.
The BP is keeping the brain perfused.
Brief hyperventilation is justified with herniation signs.

critical.explanation: Every minute of herniation damages the brainstem.
critical.kpi: Recognizes herniation and applies bridge therapy

critical.scenario: After a side-impact crash, an alert driver with a splinted leg drops from GCS 15 to 10 over 8 minutes. BP 84/56, HR 124, pale and cool. Pupils equal.
critical.question: Differential and priority?

options.t: Hemorrhagic shock reducing brain perfusion: find and treat bleeding (chest, abdomen, pelvis), pelvic binder if indicated, fluids, don't hyperventilate

options.f: Hypotension in trauma is bleeding until proven otherwise.

critical.explanation: His GCS may improve once perfusion is restored.
critical.kpi: Attributes altered mental status with hypotension to hemorrhage

critical.scenario: A 17-year-old footballer after a helmet-to-helmet hit: confused, repeating questions, can't remember the play. GCS 14, normal exam. The coach wants him back in.
critical.question: Management?

options.t: Suspected concussion: remove from play, no return today, serial neuro checks, transport for assessment, helmet on unless needed for the airway

options.f: Leave it on unless the airway needs access.
He needs assessment and a responsible adult.

critical.explanation: With neck pain or tenderness, add spinal motion restriction.
